topics.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix

value:
First,  notice that ${A}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}:$

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {a}_{1}^{T} & {a}_{2}^{T} & ⋯ & {a}_{m}^{T} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {a}_{1}^{T} \\ |\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {a}_{2}^{T} \\ |\end{bmatrix}+⋯+{x}_{m}\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {a}_{m}^{T} \\ |\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}),$ the column space of ${A}^{T},$ or equivalently, the row space of $A.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}(({A}^{T})^{T})=\text{Col}(A)$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}).$

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\hat{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\hat{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}15 & -5 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}11.8 \\ 35\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 1.1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=0.2+1.1x.$

Finally, to predict the  height after $8$ years, we substitute $x=8$ into the equation of the line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.2+1.1(8) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Since we're extrapolating ($x=8$ is not within the range of the original set of $x$-values), our result *may* be unreliable.

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=4-x-2y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4-x-2y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-x-2y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-2y⟩{|}_{z=4-x-2y} \\  & =⟨{{0}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-1)-0\cdot (-2)+(-2y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-palne is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/c1/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$

topics.title: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals

value:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

First, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:

$$
F(x,y)={{\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\frac{2xy}{(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(0,0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{1}^{2}+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2).\end{aligned}
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\hat{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\hat{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

Substituting the given values of $({X}^{T}X)^{-1}$ and ${X}^{T}y$ into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta } & =({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}\,y \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}44.5 \\ 141.5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6.5 \\ 0.8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the line $y=6.5+0.8x.$

Finally, to predict the profit in the $6$th month, we substitute $x=6$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =6.5+0.8(6) \\  & =11.3\end{aligned}
$$

So, according to the model, the profit in the $6$th month will be $$11\,300.$

title: Introduction
value:
When carrying out a linear regression in two variables, say $x$ and $y,$ our task is to find a straight line that best fits a set of data points $(x_i,y_i).$ We can easily extend this technique to situations involving three variables. 

The following table shows the number of units $x_1$ and $x_2$ (in hundreds) of two goods produced by a small company in several production runs and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) obtained by the company.   

| Good Type 1 $(x_1)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Good Type 2 $(x_2)$ | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$6$** |
| Profit $(y)$ | $6$ | $15$ | $18$ | $24$ |

Since we now have three variables, $x_1, x_2,$ and $y,$ our task is to find a *plane* of the form

$$
y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
$$

that best fits the data.

![](images/ce/ced34ebf098fd20194fafd74f4f75bf855707ad1457e706264c9e922a7efa706.png)

  

Substituting the values of $x_1$ and $x_2$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}+2{\beta }_{2}=6 \\ {\beta }_{0}+2{\beta }_{1}+3{\beta }_{2}=15 \\ {\beta }_{0}+3{\beta }_{1}+4{\beta }_{2}=18 \\ {\beta }_{0}+4{\beta }_{1}+6{\beta }_{2}=24\end{aligned}
$$

This system can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ 18 \\ 24\end{aligned}]}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

As usual, $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the coefficient vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

Since our points do not all lie on a plane, there will be no parameters $\beta_0,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the plane that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the plane of best fit (regression plane) is 

$$
y = 2+ 7x_1-x_2.
$$

    

Note that we can use the same technique to fit data involving more variables. For example, if we have four variables $x_1, x_2, x_3,$ and $y,$ then we can find a four-dimensional **hyperplane** of the form

$$
y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3
$$

that best fits a set of data points $(x_{1i},x_{2i}, x_{3i}, y).$  The coefficients of this hyperplane are found by solving the corresponding least-squares problem. 

Finally, applying linear regression to situations involving three or more variables is called **multiple linear regression**.

\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$
![](images/82/824c39c97bb115768856d672b39be8f65d8b4ecbc2ee5d6ccc9f4943594cbacd.svg)

In this new system, the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_1$ correspond to the first-row entries of $R,$ the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_2$ correspond to the second-row entries of $R,$ and the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_3$ correspond to the third-row entries of $R.$ Therefore,

![](images/5b/5ba9887a4d9b47963af171e9275319a2564eca5a4ef8b3ef44978e2ff4b111d9.svg)

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we were to expand this matrix product, we would obtain our system of equations.

title: An Illustration of How To Extend Green’s Theorem to Regions Containing Holes
value:
When proving Green's theorem, we typically start by assuming that $D$ is a so-called **simple region** (that is, a region that is both type I and type II). Then, Green's theorem is *extended* to include regions that are not simple.

Let's suppose that we've proved that Green's theorem is true for type I and type II regions. How can we use this to show that Green's theorem is also true for regions containing holes?

To illustrate how this is done, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

 

where $D$ is the annular region below.

![](images/57/57c22c3d7a92ce4a1a1a798f7e6a861ded2e9a6be4d8d98c36869fe29e2783d0.png)

Note that $\partial D= C_1\cup C_2$ is positively oriented. 

Now, imagine splitting $D$ into two regions $D_1$ and $D_2$ by means of *cuts* along the segments $[-4, -2]$ and $[2,4]$ on the $x$-axis, as shown below 

![](images/e7/e7f0d41c3fb909073cdaf4ea23f4ab617032e0d24bdc8d9b9e3724e7d56abe3b.png)

Notice that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are positively oriented type I regions. In addition, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1} & ={C}_{3}\cup {C}_{8} \\ {C}_{2} & ={C}_{5}\cup {C}_{10} \\ ∂{D}_{1} & ={C}_{3}\cup {C}_{4}\cup {C}_{5}\cup {C}_{6}, \\ ∂{D}_{2} & ={C}_{8}\cup (-{C}_{6})\cup {C}_{10}\cup (-{C}_{4})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the circulation of $\mathbf F$ over $\partial D$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup \,{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{8}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{5}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{10}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & +{{{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{4}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{6}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{-{C}_{6}}F\cdot \text{d}r}_{⏟}}_{0} \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{5}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{6}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & +{\int }_{{C}_{8}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{6}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{10}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{-{C}_{4}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={∮}_{∂{D}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{∂{D}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={∮}_{∂{D}_{1}}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y+{∮}_{∂{D}_{2}}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To summarize,

$$
\oint \limits_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = \iint_\limits{D}\left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is just Green's theorem for the region $D.$

title: Regression Planes Passing Through the Origin
value:
Sometimes, we might need to place a constraint on the regression plane that forces it to pass through the origin. 

Let's once again consider our small company. The following table shows the number of units $x_1$ and $x_2$ (in hundreds) of two goods produced by the company in several production runs and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) obtained by the company.   

| Good Type 1 $(x_1)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Good Type 2 $(x_2)$ | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$6$** |
| Profit $(y)$ | $6$ | $15$ | $18$ | $24$ |

It's known that the profit equals zero when the company does not produce any goods, so $y=0$ when $x_1=x_2 = 0.$ The company wishes to find a plane that best fits the data *subject to* the constraint that it should pass through the point $(0,0, 0).$

Therefore, we want to find the plane

$$
y = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

Substituting the values of $x_1$ and $x_2$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ 18 \\ 24\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

The rest of the arguments are the same as before. Since not all points lie on a plane, there will be no parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

title: Using Stokes' Theorem to Evaluate Line Integrals
value:
Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

![](images/fd/fd25c80fd757477b724b320d1941c57630ec1c64f36bdb44d4c1c70c526fa2a9.svg)

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface.

title: Evaluating Numerical Expressions With a Mix of Operations
value:
When an expression contains a mix of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, the order of operations tells us:

- First, we *multiply* and *divide* from left to right.
- Then, we *add* and *subtract* from left to right.

Let's use the order of operations to evaluate the expression $18 - 9 \div 3$.

First, we multiply and divide, from left to right:

$$
\begin{aligned}
18 - 9 \div 3_(⏟)_(1st) &= 18 - 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we add and subtract from left to right:

$$
\begin{aligned}
18 - 3 &= 15✓
\end{aligned}

topics.title: Variation of Parameters for Second-Order ODEs

value:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x)y_1(x)+u_2(x)y_2(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2 y_2'.
$$

Here, $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_1 = e^{x}, \qquad y_2 = e^{-6x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for $y_p,$ we get

$$
y_p =u_1e^{x}+u_2e^{-6x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for $y_p',$ we get

$$
y_p' =u_1(e^{x})'+u_2 (e^{-6x})'.
$$

Next, we substitute $y = y_p$ and $y' = y_p'$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-6y & =p(x) \\ ({y}_{p}^{′})^{′}+5{y}_{p}^{′}-6{y}_{p} & =p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Using our expressions for $y_p$ and $y_p',$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-6x})^{′})}^{′}+5({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-6x})^{′})-6({u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}) & =p(x) \\ {({u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x})}^{′}+5{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-30{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}-6{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} & =p(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-6x}+36{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} \\ \,+5{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-30{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}-6{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} & =p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group all terms proportional to $u_1$ and $u_2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}{{({e}^{x}+5{e}^{x}-6{e}^{x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{2}{{(36{e}^{-6x}-30{e}^{-6x}-6{e}^{-6x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-6x}=p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the expressions in parentheses are both zero. Therefore, the equation reduces to

$$
u_1'e^{x} - 6u_2'e^{-6x} = p(x).
$$

**Part 1**

People are entering the mall at a rate of $r(t) = 300t^2+50.$ To find out how many people entered the mall between $t=0$ and $t=2,$ we integrate $r(t)$ between these two limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}r(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}300{t}^{2}+50\,\text{d}t \\  & ={100{t}^{3}+50t|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(100\cdot {2}^{3}+50(2))-(0) \\  & =(800+100) \\  & =900\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Part 2**

People are entering the mall at a rate of $r(t) = 300t^2+50$ people per hour, and are leaving the mall at a rate of $25$ people per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** in the number of people inside the mall, which we'll call $R(t),$ is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-25\end{aligned}
$$

To find the **net change** in the number of people, we integrate $R(t)$ between $t=0$ and $t=2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}R(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}r(t)-25\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{{\int }_{0}^{2}r(t)\,\text{d}t}_{⏟}}_{900}-{\int }_{0}^{2}25\,\text{d}t \\  & =900-[25t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =900-50 \\  & =850\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, over the first two hours, there was a net increase of $850$ people.

title: Finding Total Amounts Given Rates of Change
value:
If we're interested to find the **total number** or **total amount** of some quantity, we should use the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Let's go back to the earlier example with the shopping mall (Example 1). Suppose that there are $2\,000$ people inside the mall at the moment that it opened. How many people in total are inside the mall after $2$ hours?

We already know that the **rate of change** in the number of people is $R(t).$ Therefore, the **total number of people** in the mall at time $t$, which we'll call $T(t)$ is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}r(x)-25\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: You'll notice that we changed the variable of integration from $t$ to $x.$ This is to ensure that $T$ comes out as a function of $t,$ and also so we don't get confused. When we have a definite integral, it does not matter which variable we use!

This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x=e^t,$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x=e^t,$ we note that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm d t} = e^t = x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm d t}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac1x.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+y=t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous ODE equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing.

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is 

$$
y_c(x) = A\cos t+B\sin t.
$$

Since right-hand side of the inhomogeneous ODE is a polynomial of degree $1,$ we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
y_p(t)=\alpha t+ \beta
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p$ gives:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}t} = \alpha
,\qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}t^2} = 0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
0+(\alpha t+\beta)=t
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\alpha &=1\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of [math]t[/math]}) \\ \beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system has the solution $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0.$ 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(t) = t.
$$

Now, all that remains is to write the above solution in terms of the original variable $x.$ Since $x=e^t,$ we have $t = \ln x,$ and therefore

$$
y_p(x) =\ln x.
$$

We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2000, and November 1st, 2000. 

- There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 4th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+29(1)}}+3.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(29)+3 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(1)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡14\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as January 1st, 2000, namely Saturday.

- The sum and product properties. If

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(k)\,\text{as}\,x\to a

then

$$

- The constant multiple property. If 

$$
f=O(cg)\,\text{as}\,x\to a

then

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.

$$
f=O(f)\,\text{as}\,x\to a

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

then

$$

$$
f=O(g+h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a

value:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y & x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y+1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y+1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+x)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡y+1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y+1 & -x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3} & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{3})=2{y}^{3}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=6x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{3})=6x{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=6{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{3} & 6x{y}^{2} \\ 6x{y}^{2} & 6{x}^{2}y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=2\cdot 6-6\cdot 6=-24.
$$

value:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $2\cdot 2=4$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](images/3a/3aa82e021a1871bd17abfd72570452bc6aefe358a8fddd3cb8e92bb6ff91c5a9.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{11\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $4$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{4\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}},\,{{[\frac{4\pi }{3},\frac{11\pi }{6}]}_{⏟}}_{4\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{6}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{11\pi /6}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}\theta 
$$

title: Converting From Hexadecimal to Decimal
value:
To convert a hexadecimal number to a decimal number, we expand it using the same method as decimal numbers. However, instead of using powers of $10$, we use powers of $16$.

For example, consider the following hexadecimal integer:

$$
{\color{SandyBrown}1}\,{\color{Purple}\textrm{C}}\,{\color{SteelBlue}\textrm{A}}
$$

The powers of $16$ that correspond to the digits of this number are:

| **Place Values** | $16^2$ | $16^1$ | $16^0$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Digits** | ${\color{SandyBrown}1}$ | ${\color{Purple}\textrm{C}}$ | ${\color{SteelBlue}\textrm{A}}$ |

topics.title: Solving Homogeneous Systems of ODEs With Complex Eigenvalues

value:
For a $2 \times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 

we know that if $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, the general solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

This formula works even when the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome.

A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\  & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned}
$$

The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts:

$$
\mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t)
$$

**Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$

The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following:

- For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent.

- Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution.

So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all.

Let's see a concrete example.

In a previous lesson, we learned how to convert between decimal integers and integers in base $b$, where

$$
b= 2,\, 3\, \ldots, \, 9
$$

Let's now learn how we can write a fractional number in any base.

For example, consider the following floating point fractional number in base $4{:}$

$$
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SandyBrown}1}\,.\,\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{Purple}2}\,\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SteelBlue}3}
$$

To interpret this number, we use the place value system as usual. But now, instead of *decimal* place values (that correspond to powers of *ten*), we will use a base-$4$ place values (that correspond to the powers of *four*):

| **Place Values** | $4^0$ | . | $4^{-1}$ | $4^{-2}$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Digits** | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SandyBrown}1}$ | . | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{Purple}2}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SteelBlue}3}$ |

In the place-value chart above:

- The digit $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SandyBrown}1}$ is in the $4^0$s place.
- The digit $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{Purple}2}$ is in the $4^{-1}$s place.
- The digit $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{SteelBlue}3}$ is in the $4^{-2}$s place.

Notice that place values to the right of the dot $(\,.)$ correspond to negative powers of $4$ in descending order.

Therefore, our number can be written in base $10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1.23)_{4} &= 1 \cdot 4^{0}^(⏞)^(whole) + 2 \cdot 4^{-1} + 3 \cdot 4^{-2}^(⏞)^(fraction) \\
&= 1 + 0.5 + 0.1875 \\
&= (1.6875)_{10}
\end{aligned}
$$

Any base $b$ number can be converted into a decimal number, and any decimal number can be written as a base $b$ number.

topics.title: The Joint CDF of Two Discrete Random Variables

value:
Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}\times \{3,6,9,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/04/045903aeef84fbd38d09e97f203d9169f0c1f10b662e343b82fc8113dbd1ecc3.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/81/8107e3dbe0cd180f8ce4ac8760f3fb341cb6d4accf1c698856aec361d4db23b7.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(10,9).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(10,6)$ and $(8,9).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(8,6).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(8<X\le 10,6<Y\le 9) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(10,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 10,Y\le 6)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,9)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 9)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 6)}} \\  & =F(10,9)-F(10,6)-F(8,9)+F(8,6) \\  & =0.72-0.3-0.15+0.08 \\  & =0.35.\end{aligned}
$$

title: The Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix
value:
We can write an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $A$ in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Specifically, if $\mathbf{u}_i$ denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then

$$
A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.
$$

Expressing a symmetric matrix $A$ in this way is called the **spectral decomposition** of $A.$

To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/40/408e7471e4ef788758d423af97f5683186f79192fd8933c350d45bb87f089875.svg)

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 = 6$ and $\lambda_2 = -4,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are

![](images/0c/0c22f7dd97e83c358cb3cef1fcc2db902d908140109334a8cf1c22b35b29c6d2.svg)

The spectral decomposition of $A$ is given by

$$
A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,
$$

where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spectral decomposition of $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{6}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{1}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{9}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}}+{{(-4)}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{2}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this decomposition, the matrix $\mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T$ is the orthogonal projection matrix that maps any $\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf u_i.$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

value:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $2$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option III is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

topics.title: Mean and Variance of the Negative Binomial Distribution

value:
The variance of $X$ is determined by the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{r(1-p)}{p^2}
$$

Again, it's worth comparing this to the variance of $X_{\textrm G}\sim \textrm{Geom}(p)$. Recall that

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_{\textrm G}] = \dfrac{(1-p)}{p^2}
$$

It's easy to see how the two rules are related. First, we can think of $X$ as a sum of $r$ independent geometric random variables:

$$
X = \underbrace{X_{\textrm{G}_1} + X_{\textrm{G}_2} +\cdots + X_{\textrm{G}_r}}_{r \textrm{times}}
$$

where $X_{\textrm{G}_1}, X_{\textrm{G}_2}, \ldots, X_{\textrm{G}_r} \sim \textrm{Geom}(p)$. By the properties of variance for sums of independent random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Var[X] &= Var[X_{G_{1}}] + Var[X_{G_{2}}] + ⋯ + Var[X_{G_{r}}] \\
&= ((1 - p))/(p^{2}) + ((1 - p))/(p^{2}) + ⋯ + ((1 - p))/(p^{2})_(⏟)_(rtimes) \\
&= (r(1 - p))/(p^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

title: Relationship Between Local and Global Truncation Errors
value:
How do local errors build to grow into global errors?

Again, suppose a numerical method advances the solution using the increment formula

$$
\Delta y = \Phi(x, y, \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

for some function $\Phi.$

- LTE $\tau_n$ measures the error made in *one step*, where the step begins from the exact value $y(x_{n-1}).$

- GTE $e_n$ measures the accumulated error after *many steps*, starting from $x_0$ and using the numerical method recursively.

So, at each step, we can think of the GTE as a combination of

- the total accumulated error from the previous steps ($e_{n-1}$),

- the way the method propagates these errors forward, and

- a new error introduced in the current step ($\tau_n$).

In particular, the global truncation error satisfies the following:

$$
e_n = e_{n-1} + \left[ \Phi(x_{n-1}, y(x_{n-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{n-1}, y_{n-1}, \Delta x)\right] \cdot \Delta x + \tau_n
$$

Indeed, using the iterative notation, at step $n,$ the local truncation error is

$$
\begin{aligned}{τ}_{n} & =y({x}_{n})-(y({x}_{n-1})+Φ({x}_{n-1},y({x}_{n-1}),Δx)\cdot Δx).\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging, we get an expression for the exact value $y(x_n){:}$

$$
y(x_n) = y(x_{n-1}) + \Phi(x_{n-1}, y(x_{n-1}), \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x + \tau_n
$$

Then, substituting this expression into the equation for GTE, we obtain our recursion:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{n} & =y({x}_{n})-{y}_{n} \\  & =y({x}_{n})-({y}_{n-1}+Δ{y}_{n-1}) \\  & =[y({x}_{n-1})+Φ({x}_{n-1},y({x}_{n-1}),Δx)\cdot Δx+{τ}_{n}]-[{y}_{n-1}+Φ({x}_{n-1},{y}_{n-1},Δx)\cdot Δx] \\  & =(y({x}_{n-1})-{y}_{n-1})+(Φ({x}_{n-1},y({x}_{n-1}),Δx)-Φ({x}_{n-1},{y}_{n-1},Δx))\cdot Δx+{τ}_{n} \\  & ={{{e}_{n-1}}_{⏟}}_{\text{GTE at step [math]n-1[/math]}}+{{[Φ({x}_{n-1},y({x}_{n-1}),Δx)-Φ({x}_{n-1},{y}_{n-1},Δx)]\cdot Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{propagation of }{e}_{n-1}}+{{{τ}_{n}}_{⏟}}_{\text{LTE at step [math]n[/math]}}\end{aligned}
$$

The diagram below illustrates this propagation, where $\Delta y_n$ is the increment produced by the numerical method at step $n$ starting from the previous numerical value $y_{n-1},$ while $\Delta y$ is the increment produced by the same formula but starting from the exact value $y(x_{n-1}).$

title: Explanation of the Components of Acceleration
value:
Let's suppose that the position of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t), z(t) \right\rangle.$$

Recall that the unit tangent vector is given by

$$\mathbf T = \dfrac{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf r}{\textrm{d}t}}{\left\Vert\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf r}{\textrm{d}t}\right\Vert} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{||\mathbf{v}||}.$$

Rearranging, we have

$$\mathbf{v} = ||\mathbf{v}||\mathbf T.$$

Differentiating gives

$$\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(||\mathbf{v}||)\mathbf T + ||\mathbf{v}||\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}t}.$$

Now, from the definition of the normal vector $\mathbf{N}$, notice that

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}t} = \left\Vert\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}t}\right\Vert\mathbf N = \kappa ||\mathbf{v}||\mathbf N,$$

where $\kappa$ is the curvature. Putting this into our equation for acceleration, we get

$$\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(||v||)T+||v||\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t} \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(||v||)T+||v||(κ||v||N) \\ & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(||v||)}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{T}}T+{{κ||v|{|}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{N}}N \\ & ={a}_{T}T+{a}_{N}N.\end{aligned}$$

This means that the acceleration of the particle lies in the osculating plane spanned by $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{N},$ where the tangential component is the coefficient of $\mathbf{T}$ and the normal component is the coefficient of $\mathbf{N}.$

Indeed, taking the dot product of $\mathbf{T}$ with $\mathbf{a}$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}T\cdot a & =T\cdot ({a}_{T}T+{a}_{N}N) \\ & ={a}_{T}(T\cdot T)+{a}_{N}(T\cdot N) \\ & ={a}_{T}.\end{aligned}$$

Therefore,

$$a_T = \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{||\mathbf{v}||}.$$

Also, crossing $\mathbf{T}$ with $\mathbf{a},$ we get

$$\begin{aligned}T\times a & =T\times ({a}_{T}T+{a}_{N}N) \\ & ={a}_{T}(T\times T)+{a}_{N}(T\times N) \\ & ={a}_{N}(T\times N).\end{aligned}$$

Taking the norm of both sides and remembering that $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{N}$ are orthogonal unit vectors, we have that

$$\begin{aligned}||T\times a|| & =||{a}_{N}(T\times N)|| \\ & ={a}_{N}||T\times N|| \\ & ={a}_{N}||T||||N||\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ & ={a}_{N}\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\ & ={a}_{N}.\end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$$a_N = ||\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{a}|| = \dfrac{||\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{a}||}{||\mathbf{v}||}.$$

title: A Special Case of the Multivariable Chain Rule
value:
There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Showing That a Geometric Distribution Is a Probability Distribution
value:
You might be wondering where the geometric distribution gets its name. The answer is that the probability mass function forms a geometric sequence! 

Suppose that $X\sim \textrm{Geom}(p).$ Then, the probability mass function for this geometric distribution is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-p)^{x-1}p \\ f(x) & =p(1-p)^{x-1} \\ {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{x}} & ={{p}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}\cdot ({{1-p}_{⏟}}_{r})^{x-1} \\ {a}_{x} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we see that the probability mass function can be interpreted as a geometric sequence where the first term is $a_1=p,$ and the common ratio is $r=1-p.$

Moreover, notice that $f(x)$ satisfies all the criteria to be a probability mass function, namely

1\. $0 \leq f(x) \leq 1$ for all $x$ in $S$

2\. $\displaystyle \sum\limits_{x \in S} f(x) = 1$

Criterion 1 is clearly true because $0 \leq p \leq 1.$ 

To show that criterion 2 is true, we simply need to calculate the sum of this infinite geometric series, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{x\in S}f(x) & ={\sum }_{x=1}^{\infty }p(1-p)^{x-1} \\  & =\frac{p}{1-(1-p)} \\  & =\frac{p}{p} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is indeed a probability distribution.

value:
We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity. 

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and

- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

Recall that a random variable's probability distribution is uniquely determined by its moment-generating function (MGF). Therefore, if the MGF of a random variable $X$ matches that of a known distribution, then $X$ has the same distribution.

For a binomial random variable $Y_i \sim \textrm{B}(n,p)$, we have

$$
M_{Y_i}(t) = (1-p+pe^t)^n
$$

In our case, since $Y_i \sim \textrm{B}(5,0.3)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{Y_{i}}(t) &= (1 - 0.3 + 0.3e^{t})^{5} \\
&= (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

If

$$
Y = Y_1+Y_2+\cdots + Y_{10}
$$

where $Y_1, Y_2,\ldots Y_{10}$ are independent random variables with moment-generating function $M_{Y_i}(t)$, then the moment-generating function of $Y$ is

$$
M_Y(t) = M_{Y_1}(t) \cdot M_{Y_2}(t) \cdots M_{Y_{10}}(t)
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{Y}(t) &= (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5} \cdot (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}⋯(0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}^(⏞)^(10times) \\
&= (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{50}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $M_Y(t)$ is the MGF of a binomial random variable with $n = 50$ and $p= 0.3$.

Therefore, we conclude that $Y\sim B(50,0.3)$.

An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_1$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u+v \\ v-2u+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u+v \\ -2u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ v-u\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ -u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

In fact, the transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is a linear transformation.

- Transformation $\mathbf{T}_3$ is not affine since it contains the quadratic term $v^2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{T}_1$ and $\mathbf{T}_2$ only."

We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=80.6+5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=80.6+5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(T>4.303)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.025}=4.303.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(3-6)^{2}+(5-6)^{2}+(7-6)^{2}+(9-6)^{2} \\  & =9+1+1+9 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=4.303\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.35}{20}}≈0.6
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=5\pm 0.6
$$

title: Introduction

A square matrix $A$ is **orthogonally diagonalizable** if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Note that this is equivalent to the equation

$$
D = P^TAP.
$$

So, to orthogonally diagonalize a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ that satisfies the above equations.

A helpful theorem allows us to determine whether a real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. It states the following:

*A matrix $A$ with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.*

Consequently, *every* symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable!

For example, the symmetric matrix 

![](images/b3/b3970eb885720ce2aa4394918c6c5f9f343e26aa60039df219abf56398f096db.svg)

has the orthogonal diagonalization

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={{[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{T}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $P$ is orthogonal, and $D$ is diagonal. As usual, the entries on the main diagonal of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A.$ Also, the columns of $P$ are *orthonormal* eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues of $A.$

The procedure of the orthogonal diagonalization of a $2 \times 2$ real symmetric matrix $A$ is almost the same as the diagonalization of a matrix:

- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$.

- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of *unit orthogonal* eigenvectors of $A.$

- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

In the case of symmetric matrices, the two eigenvectors we compute in step 2 will always be orthogonal, provided that they correspond to different eigenvalues. However, we must also ensure that we *normalize* those eigenvectors.

value:

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!
$$

This relationship holds for any natural number $n \geq 1.$ Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

For any natural number $n \geq 1,$ the above identity states the following:

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)
$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(n+1) & =nΓ(n) \\  & =n\cdot \overset{Γ(n)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-1)\cdot Γ(n-1)}} \\  & =n\cdot (n-1)\cdot \overset{Γ(n-1)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-2)\cdot Γ(n-2)}} \\  & =… \\  & ={{n\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)\cdot …\cdot 1}_{⏟}}_{n!}\cdot Γ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1).
$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1),$ we can use the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n!
$$

title: Introduction
value:
An **affine transformation** $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function that can be expressed in the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

Under this notation, 

- $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}$ represents vectors belonging to the input space, and

- $\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}$  represents vectors belonging to the output space.

For example,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}
$$

is an affine transformation because it can be expressed in the form $\mathbf x = A\mathbf u + \mathbf b,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v+1 \\ 2u+v-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ 2u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the transformation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}
$$

is not affine since it contains the quadratic term $uv.$

Finally, note the following relationships between affine and linear transformations:

- A linear transformation $\mathbf x = A \mathbf u$ is a special case of an affine transformation with $\mathbf b = \mathbf 0.$

- For an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ given by $\mathbf x = A\mathbf u + \mathbf b,$ we say that $A$ is *the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with* $\mathbf T.$

title: Proof of the Recursive Formula
value:
Here, we'll prove the recursive formula for the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(z+1) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }-z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})-{(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})|}_{t=0}+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =0-0+z{{{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t}_{⏟}}_{Γ(z)} \\  & =zΓ(z)\end{aligned}
$$

title: Derivation of the Axis of Symmetry Formula

topics.title: Writing the Equation of a Parabola in Vertex Form

value:
**Note**: You may find the algebra in this section a little tricky. It's a good idea to go through it, but you will not be quizzed on it. You may skip this section if you wish.

![](images/2a/2a400b12675f8ebf19ba563192d9ae2296336e40ea380d40e6247564718a2b1f.png)

You may have seen already that for the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

with

$$
a\neq 0
$$

the **axis of symmetry** of this parabola is given by the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We're now in a position to derive this formula.

Since

$$
a \neq 0
$$

we can take out a factor of $a$ from the right-hand side in the parabola formula:

$$
y = a\left(x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + \dfrac{c}{a} \right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract*

$$
\left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2{:}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2+{\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}x + \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2}_{\textrm{perfect square}} - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2+ {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{2a}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}\dfrac{c}{a}}
$$

Simplifying the last two terms, we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 - \dfrac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2} = \left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a} \right)^2 + \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}
$$

Next, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a((x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}}) &= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + a \cdot \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a^{2}} \\
&= a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a} \\
&= a(x - (-\frac{b}{2a})_(⏟)_(h))^{2} + \frac{4ac - b^{2}}{4a}_(⏟)_(k)
\end{aligned}
$$

By denoting

$$
h=-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \qquad k=\dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a}
$$

we get the equation of the parabola in vertex form:

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

where the vertex is given by

$$
(h,k) = \left(-\dfrac{b}{2a}, \dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a} \right)
$$

Finally, since the parabola's axis of symmetry is the vertical line passing through the vertex, the equation of the axis must be

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

title: Forming a Basis Using Generalized Eigenvectors
value:
So, not every $n\times n$ matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$

Despite this, we have the following theorem:

*For any real $n \times n$ matrix, there is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.*

To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix 
![](images/d0/d09805a20bbc23954fdec5a893e05ec0bad45a6503e27354df60b4d71952f990.svg)

where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$ are

![](images/e6/e6053d03e5e0f4bc843856d88dbc9e8e14252200a5d7280a4a05872b19bd4d56.svg)

Remember that $\lambda = 4$ has *algebraic* multiplicity $3$ and *geometric* multiplicity $2.$

Now, it's easy to show that $A$ has a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ given by

![](images/89/890d3b69aa88f0f442760d03afc7333d2e918b5b3401a33b167cfa40321a5f4c.svg)
and our generalized eigenvectors form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, ${\color{blue}{\mathbf{u}}}, {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}},$ and $\color{red}\mathbf{w}$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ In particular, our basis consists of

- two eigenvectors ($\color{blue}\mathbf{u}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$), and

- one generalized eigenvector whose rank is greater than one ($\color{red}\mathbf{w}$).

Notice that the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{algebraic multiplicity}-\text{geometric multiplicity} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is no coincidence. In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$*

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v+7 \\ u+v+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the endpoints of $\overline{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overline{P'Q'}.$ So, to find the image of $\overline{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

value:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v+2 \\ 4u-5v+9\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ 4u-5v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 9\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 4 & -5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-5)-(-1)\cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y-9\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9) \\ 4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5x-y-1 \\ 4x-y+1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{5}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{(-1)}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{4}x - y + 1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = 5 + (-1) + 4 = 8.
$$

value:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=-2.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $det(A)<0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is not orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

topics.title: The Inverse of an Affine Transformation

value:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=(-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=-2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u \\ u-v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1=-1\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3u+6v \\ u+2v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot 2-6\cdot 1=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only."

value:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5v-7u+3 \\ 7v-10u+5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7u+5v \\ -10u+7v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 5 \\ -10 & 7\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{7\cdot (-7)-5\cdot (-10)}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-3 \\ y-5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7\cdot (x-3)+(-5)\cdot (y-5) \\ 10\cdot (x-3)+(-7)\cdot (y-5)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7x-5y+4 \\ 10x-7y+5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7x-5y+4,\,v=10x+(-7)y+5.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=7+10+(-7)=10.
$$

An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}v-u \\ u+v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u+v \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=-2.
$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|det(A)|=|-2|=2.
$$

Let's consider a few powers of $2$ and their corresponding binary notations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2^{0} &= (1)_{2} \\
2^{1} &= (10)_{2} \\
2^{2} &= (100)_{2} \\
2^{3} &= (1000)_{2} \\
&= ⋮ \\
