$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-4y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,4,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-4y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨x-4y+1,\,x+1,\,-y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(x-4y+1-4(x+1)+y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}(-3x-3y-3) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-x-y-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(C),$ we need to check if the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[C\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[C\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 & -4 & 9 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & -8 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & -8 \\ 4 & 1 & -4 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 4 & 1 & -4 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -7 & -16 & -11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{7}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 & -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=-3 \\ -9{x}_{3} &=-18.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2}+3(2) & =-3 \\ {x}_{2} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\  & =5-2(-3)-3(2) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(C).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}:$

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}=5\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{1}}+(-3)\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{2}}+2\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{3}}
$$

Finally, we get ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=5\cdot (-3)\cdot 2=-30.$

value:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{3}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

value:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

topics.title: The Second Derivative of a Multivariable Function

value:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2} & -2y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2})=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

value:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡x & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-\frac{\pi }{2},1)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2xy+{y}^{2} & {x}^{2}+2xy\end{bmatrix},$ 
 we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy+{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}+2xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+{y}^{2})=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy)=2x+2y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{y}^{2})=2x+2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy)=2x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x+2y \\ 2x+2y & 2x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(-1,2).$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(-1,2)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=\frac{2y}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{2y}{x} & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=(-1)\cdot 0-2\cdot 2=-4.
$$

value:
We know that any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the coordinates relative to the basis $\,B.$ Since we are told that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={{(\,3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{{(\,-3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -24 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -12 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -36 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$

$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

value:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y+1}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y+1}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(x+y+1)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(x+y+1)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(x+y+1)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+1\cdot x+1\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+1x+1y-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{2})xy-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{n}$ of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{n}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{n-1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }…\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{n-1},{v}_{n-2},…,{v}_{1}\ne 0.$ An *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & x+2y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2y)=1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2} & 2y{x}^{2}-1\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}-1.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2}-1)=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=2\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-12.
$$

$$

$$

Now, we multiply:

$$
10\times 2=20

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{12}.$

Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{6}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{12}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}})\cdot (2\sqrt{3})=\sqrt{2}.$

$$

Therefore, $32\times 32=1\,024.$

There is $1$ decimal place in the first factor ($3.2$) and $1$ decimal place in the second factor ($3.2$), so their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

$$

$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$

$$

$$

The average value of a function on a given interval $[a,b]$ is 

$$
{f}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the additive property of the definite integral, we write

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}.
$$

The 1st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,0].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-4.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-6.

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}-{A}_{2} \\  & =-4-6 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}

Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{8}(xy)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{8}{y}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{8}{y}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{8}{y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [0,2].$

- Statement II is true. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{9}{8}(xy)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{8}{x}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{8}{x}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,1].$ So, when $x\in [0,1]$ and $y\in [0,2],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{\frac{9}{8}(xy)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}={{(3{x}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{(\frac{3}{8}{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

topics.title: The Second Derivative of a Multivariable Function

value:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,2).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,2)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/cd/cdb5c8084958ba3dc1175c1e92035d89fb4edcdf8ce333962b49f22b40552f71.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the infinite rectangle with its top-right corner at $(5,1)$ and top-left corner at $(3,1),$ where the top and right boundaries are included, and the left boundary is excluded.

![](images/1c/1c28f3e2f820511a30aa64ccd3affacaa6d72e69da9c596827429b244bf1129a.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(5,1)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/ae/ae993ae6e8c0d71a42ca0e11ed5b30a8d762b3fab12771247eca262f0131c4f5.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3,Y<2) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(5,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 5,Y\le 1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(5,1)-F(3,1) \\  & =0.67-0.43 \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\hat{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={(\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\hat{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\hat{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\hat{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\hat{x}-b & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\hat{x}-b‖=\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{35}.
$$

We need to write and evaluate an expression representing the total number of pies.

Since each of them baked $2$ cherry pies and $3$ apple pies, the number of pies each person made is:

$$
{{2}_{⏟}}_{\text{cherry pies}}+{{3}_{⏟}}_{\text{apple pies}}
$$

Since *each* person made this number of pies, and there are $3$ people, we must multiply the number of pies by $3.$ Therefore, the total number of pies is:

$$
{{(2+3)}_{⏟}}_{\text{each person}}\times {{3}_{⏟}}_{\text{people}}
$$

To evaluate the expression, we follow the order of operations with parentheses.

First, we perform the operations inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2+3)\times 3 & =(2+3)\times 3 \\  & =5\times 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply:

$$
5\times 3=15
$$

value:
Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/62/6287f4884b335466bc7e1d6da17190f32d447f065e37a37e79a1aa48a6109415.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(4,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(2,-1)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/d4/d4d76ca2e80bccda9cbcfa4e28c628dffcec62b3fb42d62f9315fce2623e12fe.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X<4,-1\le Y<1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le -1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(4,1)-F(4,-1)-F(2,1)+F(2,-1) \\  & =0.8-0.2-0.3+0.1 \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

topics.title: The Joint CDF of Two Discrete Random Variables

value:
Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/77/7790a013e37bb86c00b44b1c022d6597f9bbdd57616c48e7ee7dfe8ddf512c63.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/65/6535c5bf152e8a9b09bf5522cdc442668add6c4cc7a0df4e07307f9931886a80.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(9,10).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(9,4)$ and $(6,10).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(6,4).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6<X\le 9,4<Y\le 10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 4)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 4)}} \\  & =F(9,10)-F(9,4)-F(6,10)+F(6,4) \\  & =0.8-0.3-0.4+0.2 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}} \\ Ax & =b\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\hat{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{45}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\hat{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\hat{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\hat{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A\hat{x}-b & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
‖A\hat{x}-b‖=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\sqrt{3}.
$$

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)=\{0\} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $y=z,$ any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $Tx=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has no solution, this means that $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\notin \text{Im}(T).$ Therefore, $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{3}$ and, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

value:
We're given that $g(x)=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x)>0.$ Now, recall the following:

- If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

Let's now consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- Statement II is false. Differentiating $g(x)=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}-2)^{′}\cdot f(x)+({x}^{2}-2)\cdot {f}^{′}(x) \\  & =2x\cdot f(x)+({x}^{2}-2)\cdot {f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x)$ is negative and strictly increasing over the interval $(0,1),$ we have 

$$
2x>0,\,f(x)<0,\,{x}^{2}-2<0,\,{f}^{′}(x)>0.
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
{g}^{′}(x)={{2x}_{⏟}}_{>0}\cdot {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}+{{({x}^{2}-2)}_{⏟}}_{<0}\cdot {{{f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}={{2x\cdot f(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}+\,{{{x}^{2}\cdot {f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}<0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${g}^{′}(x)<0,$ the function $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing. Therefore, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & {e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,0)=(-1)\cdot 1-{0}^{2}=-1.
$$

We're given that $g(x)={x}^{3}\cdot f(x)>0.$ Now, recall the following:

- If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y & 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,\pi ).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,\pi )=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Finally, we get

$$

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$

$$

$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{y}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+{e}^{y}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{x{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-1)=1.
$$

$$

$$

 
where $y\in [1,2].$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4{x}^{3},\end{aligned}

topics.title: Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices

value:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-1)}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

topics.title: The Second Derivative of a Multivariable Function

value:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(10+x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{number of children enrolled}}\times \,\,\,\,\,\,{{(40-2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{monthly fee}} \\  & =(10+x)(40-2x) \\  & =400-20x+40x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =400+20x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the center can only take care between $10$ and $20$ children, the permitted domain for $x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & \le x+10\le 20 \\ 0 & \le x\le 10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $0<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=20-4x,
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 20-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =20 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=5$ lies in the interval $0<x<10.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=5$ does indeed give a maximum value of $R(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{R}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=5$ is indeed a local maximum of $R(x).$ And since $R(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=5$ is a global maximum of $R(x).$

topics.title: Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices

value:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{3}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{3}{4}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{3}{4} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

value:
Recall that $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the probability that the pair $(X,Y)$ will lie inside the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/15/1524afeeaea3cc0fd4ee51b9572222bdd846fba378e029e4fa20a272a4fe6353.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(8,6).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(8,2)$ and $(2,6).$

3\. Finally, we need to *add back* the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\le X\le 8,2\le Y\le 6) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 2)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 2)}} \\  & =F(8,6)-F(8,2)-F(2,6)+F(2,2) \\  & =0.8-0.5-0.4+0.2 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

value:
We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=61.7+6.8x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=61.7+6.8x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=61.7.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $98%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.98=0.02\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.01.
$$

We are given that $P(T>6.965)=0.01.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.01}=6.965.
$$

$$

Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{bmatrix},
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -5 \\ 5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\ne C,
$$

while

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2+5\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =\begin{bmatrix}1-4\text{i} \\ 5\text{i}\end{bmatrix}={{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=2
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2})-2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+2-2) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2}+2 & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}+\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}-{z}_{2}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the pair of intersecting lines ${z}_{2}=\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2}=-\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}.$
